newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angolan army said slowing offensive in northeast.
newsitem.headline: Angolan army said slowing offensive in northeast.

text.p: A month-long Angolan government offensive into diamond areas held by the former rebel UNITA in the northeast has slowed ahead of a United Nations Security Council meeting on Angola, military sources said on Tuesday.
"The army seems to have slowed its advance just south of Luia," said one military source, referring to a town in Lunda Norte province which fell to government forces last Friday.

The U.N. special envoy, Alioune Blondin Beye, who heads a peacekeeping force of 5,000 in Angola, left Luanda on Monday for New York to brief the Security Council this week on Angola's two-year peace process.
Western diplomats in Luanda said a tough stand by the Security Council on the government's military actions was needed to dissuade the army from continuing its advances.
"If the Security Council doesn't condemn this the army will feel like they can push on," one diplomat said.

UNITA (National Union for the Total Independence of Angola) and the government fought a two-decades long civil war that finally ended with the 1994 Lusaka accord, but implementation has been difficult.
In April UNITA and the ruling MPLA created a power-sharing government with 70 UNITA deputies taking a seat in parliament.
The former rebels however still hold on to about 70 percent of the countryside including most of the diamond fields.
The recent fighting is the worst since a ceasefire was declared in November 1994.

"The government is violating the Lusaka accord by moving into these areas," a diplomat said, adding: "UNITA has obviously violated the accord because their soldiers are fighting back while they have been telling us all along that they have abided by the peace process and demobilised all their soldiers."
Beye told Reuters on Saturday that the Angolan government had agreed to stop its military operation in the diamond areas.
But Angolan state television showed images on Sunday of army tanks, armoured troop carriers and artillery in Luia.

Government military officers told state television that 10 government soldiers had been killed and 47 wounded on June 17 during the takeover of Luia, while 58 UNITA members were killed and 23 were taken prisoner.
There was no mention of wounded on UNITA's side.
General Adriano MacKenzie, who is leading the operation in the northeast, said the aim of the offensive was to secure the country's borders from armed refugees from the neighbouring former Zaire.
"The conflict in Zaire brought many armed Rwandan and Zairean refugees into UNITA zones in this part of Angola," MacKenzie told the television.
"The government is very concerned about this and wishes to take control of this area."
MacKenzie accused UNITA of gathering men south of Luia for a counter-attack on the government.
